transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-12 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~40m | Attendees: Casey, Jordan (Redwood); Alex, Priya, Sam, Nina (HelioForge)

[00:00:00] Casey: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to go over the last sprint's bench results and align on the decision criteria for the cutover. Jordan, do you want to run us through the numbers?
[00:00:18] Jordan: Yeah, sure. Quick note — some of these numbers we pulled from the shared spreadsheet (link) that we uploaded last night. So p50 looks great, we're routinely at ~18ms for the trimmed test, but p95 spiked up to 220ms in two of the bursts and p99 hit 480ms. The incumbent, LegacyVendor, is sitting around p95 180ms and p99 420ms on the same workload.
[00:00:45] Alex: Just to be clear, these are for the 2k token prompt with KV cache primed vs cold?
[00:00:55] Jordan: Good call — we ran both. With the KV cache primed the p95 improved to 120ms often but the problem is when the burst rate increases and cache eviction happens, that tail balloons. There's also a path where quantized model variants behaved a bit differently — quantized Q4 gave us lower median but slightly worse p99 in our tests.
[00:01:20] Priya: That's interesting — are you seeing that across different sequence lengths or was this just the 2k?
[00:01:27] Jordan: Mostly 1k and 2k show it. Short sequences (256) are fine. The pattern points to cache thrash under sustained concurrency.
[00:01:38] Sam: Do we have traces for the two big spikes? I can correlate with our ingress spikes to see if client side is contributing.
[00:01:45] Jordan: We have traces, but the sampling was sparse in sprint 2. I'll re-run a focused tail-latency capture and include full traces.
[00:01:52] Nina: Also throw in the request headers; we saw some anomalous routing to a fallback in one run.

[00:02:10] Casey: On the high level tradeoff, the team asked about Dedicated slots. If we move to Dedicated we get more predictable KV lifetime and can tune autoscaling policy tightly, but that comes with commit cost. We want to make the decision based on unit economics and tail-latency risk.
[00:02:28] Alex: Price sensitivity is big. LegacyVendor gave us a blended price that's slightly lower per token but their SLAs have had intermittent incidents. If Redwood can get p95 near incumbent and show better graceful fallback, we'd be comfortable moving.
[00:02:42] Casey: Understood. Jordan, did you compare cost and latency curves when using batching and tighter continuous batching windows?
[00:02:50] Jordan: Yes — tightening batch windows from 50ms to 20ms reduced median slightly but increased tail under bursts because more small batches increase scheduling overhead. There's a sweet spot around 30ms for this workload. Also, prefix caching is helping — but HelioForge's traffic has a long tail of unique prefixes so cache hit rate is only about 52% currently.
[00:03:15] Priya: That low? We assumed cache would be higher. Our usage has a lot of user-specific context, yeah.
[00:03:20] Jordan: Right, the personalization reduces prefix reuse. We suggested some lightweight client-side normalization to raise effective reuse.

[00:03:40] Alex: On security — we're still vetting SOC2 artifacts. Any gaps we should know about from Redwood?
[00:03:46] Casey: We provided the SOC2 report in the secure folder; Jordan can also pull the Private deployment checklist. The SOC2 questions we talked about earlier — encryption at rest with customer KMS — is supported in our Private product and in Dedicated via KMS integrations.
[00:04:00] Sam: Great. Also need audit log format for our SIEM team.
[00:04:05] Jordan: We'll export an example audit log and send it.

[00:04:25] [rough cross-talk, speaker overlap] Priya: Back to the bench — what about fallback behaviour, like if a model variant isn't available?
[00:04:33] Jordan: We tested automated fallback: requests go to a smaller quantized variant with lower latency but slightly different output distribution. We also added a model quality gate that checks token-level divergence on a small eval set. In our runs fallback triggered during two bursts and raised mean token-diff by about 2.1%, which the product team flagged as acceptable for non-critical paths.
[00:05:01] Alex: Hmm, for medical content we want strict guards. We'll need a canary with label-aware evals.
[00:05:07] Casey: Makes sense — propose: canary to 1% traffic with label-aware evals for two weeks. If metrics pass, expand.

[00:05:25] Jordan: For the focused tests we propose: (1) synthetic burst at 8x baseline for 10m with primed and cold cache runs, (2) 95th/99th capture with full trace enabled, (3) routing playbook where we force a fallback to observe end-user delta. I'll run these in our lab and share the raw trace files.
[00:05:43] Sam: We'll feed the traces into our observability pipeline.

[00:06:00] Priya: What does the Dedicated slot cadence look like operationally? Like how long to spin up extra capacity?
[00:06:06] Jordan: Dedicated pools are soft-pinned; cold start for a new slot is a few minutes, warm scaling is sub-30s for adding existing instances if we provision spare capacity. But you can also buy burst credits for immediate capacity.
[00:06:22] Alex: If we need to go live quickly, what's the minimum commitment?
[00:06:27] Casey: We have monthly and annual; monthly has higher unit cost but lower commitment. For a POC we can do a 3-month pilot pricing as a bridge. I'll send numbers.

[00:06:45] [00:06:45] Jordan: One more note — quantization: we tested Q4-AA vs Q4-GG (names fuzzy) and saw the Q4-AA had better throughput but slightly higher hallucination rate on our eval prompts. Nina flagged two content regressions.
[00:07:01] Nina: The regressions were minor but consistent on prompts with numeric precision. We need to validate evals for those patterns.

[00:07:20] Priya: Can we also measure end-to-end latency including our edge transforms?
[00:07:25] Sam: Yes, we'll run a concurrent run with our edge proxies. We'll share the sidecar metrics.

[00:07:40] Casey: Recap — Jordan runs targeted tail-latency tests and shares traces; Casey sends updated pricing and Dedicated options; HelioForge to share real traffic profile and SOC2 contact. If tail-latency falls within a 10% delta of incumbent on p95/p99 under burst test and quality gates pass, we'll schedule a canary cutover.
[00:08:02] Alex: Sounds good. Timeline?
[00:08:07] Casey: Aiming for lab runs done by 2026-05-18, review call 2026-05-19, canary window week of 2026-05-25 if green.

[00:08:20] Jordan: I'll annotate the spreadsheet with the p50/p95/p99 columns and mark which runs were primed/cold and quantized. Expect raw trace link and short notes.

[00:08:32] Priya: One operational question: if we move to Dedicated and see occasional tail spikes, what's Redwood's mitigation SLA?
[00:08:38] Casey: Dedicated includes an SLA for availability and an objective on latency SLI with credits shown in the contract. We can include runbook commitments for mitigation steps (spin reserves, route by latency) in the pilot annex.

[00:08:52] Alex: Ok. Also request a sample of audit logs and a KMS key rotation policy summary.
[00:08:58] Casey: Will do.

[00:09:10] [longer pause, small talk] Alex: Appreciate the team's speed on this.
[00:09:15] Jordan: No problem. Quick practical: when we run the 8x bursts, please make sure any upstream retries are off so we don't artificially inflate traffic.
[00:09:25] Sam: Noted. We'll coordinate.

[00:09:40] Priya: One more — quality monitoring: can Redwood stream eval alerts to our webhook?
[00:09:45] Jordan: Yes; we have a webhook-based quality alerting that can be configured per alias. We'll add HelioForge as a channel.

[00:09:55] Casey: Anything else?
[00:10:00] Alex: No, that's it from me.

[00:10:05] Casey: Great. We'll follow up with the dataset and links. Thanks everyone.

[End of recorded portion — remaining minutes were follow-up coordination in email and deck updates.]
